Foundations: Goals, KPIs and SMART Targets

Before you open a spreadsheet you need to know what success looks like. This module shows the difference between being busy and making progress, how to pick a small set of key performance indicators (KPIs), and how to turn a vague hope into a SMART target with a baseline. It also covers how to keep other people's data safe from day one.

Many hardworking women end the month tired but unsure whether the business or project actually moved forward. You posted on WhatsApp every day, you ran three trainings, you answered fifty calls. Did sales rise? Did the women you trained start using what they learned? **Performance tracking** is the habit of writing down a few chosen numbers on a regular schedule so that you can answer those questions with evidence instead of feelings. **Reporting** is how you share those numbers, and what they mean, with someone else: your manager, a funder, a business partner or simply yourself.

Development organisations, government programmes and most funders describe work as a chain of four links. Once you can see the chain, you can see which numbers really show performance.

**Inputs** are the resources you use: money, flour, data bundles, your hours, a trainer's time.
**Activities** are the actions: baking, posting adverts, holding a training session, making calls.
**Outputs** are the direct products you can count straight away: 200 meat pies baked, 4 sessions held, 60 women registered.
**Outcomes** are the changes that matter: pies sold and paid for, profit earned, women who now keep written records, customers who come back.

Inputs and activities are easy to count, which is why reports are often full of them. But a report that says 'we held 12 meetings' tells the reader nothing about whether the meetings worked. Good tracking always includes at least one output and one outcome.

Worked example: busy week versus good week

For example, Bisi sells meat pies and chin chin from her kitchen in Ibadan and takes orders on WhatsApp. She feels that posting more always brings more sales, so she compares two weeks from her notebook.
Week 1: she posted 30 status updates (activity), received 12 orders (output) and collected ₦54,000 in sales (outcome).
Week 2: she was ill for two days and posted only 15 updates, yet received 14 orders and collected ₦63,000.
She divides sales by posts to see sales per post: Week 1 ₦54,000 ÷ 30 = ₦1,800 per post. Week 2 ₦63,000 ÷ 15 = ₦4,200 per post.
She looks closer and sees that in Week 2 she posted clear photos with prices and a 'order by Thursday for Saturday delivery' message, while in Week 1 many posts were greetings.
Doubling her posts did not double her sales. The type of post mattered more than the number. Without writing the numbers down, Bisi would have kept working harder on the wrong activity.

Effort still counts
Tracking activities is not wrong. You need them to understand why outcomes went up or down. The mistake is reporting effort as if it were the result.
Start with one question

Every tracking system should begin with a question that someone actually needs answered. Good questions are short and have a time frame. 'Are my weekend sales growing month by month?' 'How many of the women we trained this quarter are still saving every week?' 'Which delivery area brings in the most profit?' If you cannot say what decision the answer will help you make, you probably do not need to track that number.

Timing: outputs come fast, outcomes come slowly

Outputs usually appear the same day or week: pies baked, sessions held. Outcomes often take longer: a customer coming back for a second order, a trained woman still saving after three months. A practical rhythm is to record outputs daily or weekly and check outcomes monthly or at the end of a project phase. If you only look at outcomes, you will find problems too late. If you only look at outputs, you may never know whether the work succeeded.
Common mistake 1: counting the same thing twice, such as a customer who sent the same order by call and by WhatsApp.
Common mistake 2: mixing outputs and outcomes in one number, such as 'women reached' when some only received a flyer.
Common mistake 3: tracking a number nobody uses. If no decision depends on it, stop recording it.

A **metric** is any number you can measure. A **key performance indicator (KPI)** is one of the few metrics you have chosen because it shows, better than others, whether you are reaching your goal. A small shop might measure twenty things, but only three or four of them deserve to be KPIs. If everything is a KPI, nothing is.

Five checks for a good KPI
**Linked to the goal.** If the KPI improves, the goal is closer. Followers on Instagram may not be linked to sales; paid orders are.
**Clearly defined.** Everyone counts it the same way. Does 'customer' mean anyone who asked a price, or someone who paid?
**Measurable with data you can actually get.** If nobody records it, you cannot track it. Choose numbers that come from your sales book, transfer history or attendance register.
**Something you can influence.** Tracking the price of flour is useful, but it is not your performance. Your cost per pie is.
**Few in number.** Three to five KPIs is enough for most small teams and projects.
Watch out for vanity metrics
Likes, views and status replies feel good but often do not lead to money or change. Use them as supporting metrics, never as your main proof of performance, unless your goal truly is awareness.
Leading and lagging indicators

A **lagging indicator** tells you the result after it has happened: monthly sales, profit, number of women who completed the programme. A **leading indicator** moves earlier and helps predict the result: number of enquiries this week, number of samples given out, attendance at the first two sessions. A good KPI set mixes both, so you can see trouble coming and still prove the final result.
Ratio KPIs: turning counts into insight
Raw counts are useful, but ratios often tell you more because they allow fair comparison between weeks of different sizes. Three ratios work for almost any small business.

For example, Halima coordinates a savings-skills programme for women in a Kano community, funded by a small grant. 60 women registered, 45 attended at least four of five sessions, and 3 months later 27 of those 45 are still saving every week.

Write each KPI with a short definition beside it, for example 'Order: a sale where payment has been received'. This stops arguments later and makes your reports trustworthy.
When the boss or funder chooses the KPIs

In a job or a funded project, some KPIs are given to you. A funder may already have a results framework or logframe, a table that lists the indicators, targets and how each will be measured. Do not replace these with your own. Read the definition of each indicator carefully, ask questions if anything is unclear, and track exactly what was agreed. You can still add one or two of your own supporting metrics to help you manage the work day to day, as long as you label them clearly.

Finally, review your KPI list every few months. If your goal changes, for example from growing sales to improving profit, your KPIs should change too. Keep a note of the date and reason for any change so that later comparisons stay honest.

A KPI tells you what to measure. A **target** tells you what number you are aiming for, and by when. Without a target, a report can only say 'sales were ₦70,000'. With a target it can say 'sales were ₦70,000 against a target of ₦69,000, so we reached 101%'. That one comparison is what makes a report useful to a manager or funder.

Step 1: find your baseline

A **baseline** is where you are now, measured before you start trying to improve. Use at least four weeks of records if you have them, because one week can be unusually good or bad. If you have no records yet, track for two to four weeks first and set the target afterwards. Guessing a baseline is one of the most common reasons targets end up either impossible or meaningless.
Step 2: make the target SMART
The SMART test
Specific: what exactly?
Measurable: which number?
Achievable: realistic from baseline?
Relevant: linked to goal?
Time-bound: by when?

Worked example: from baseline to target
For example, Bisi wants her sales to grow before the festive season. Her records for the last four weeks show weekly sales of ₦52,000, ₦58,000, ₦61,000 and ₦69,000.
Baseline = ₦240,000 ÷ 4 = ₦60,000 average per week.
She chooses a 15% increase because she plans one new action (a Saturday delivery slot) and believes a small, steady rise is achievable.
SMART target: 'Raise average weekly sales from ₦60,000 to ₦69,000 for the four weeks ending 31 March, by adding a Saturday delivery slot.'
A clear number, a deadline and a planned action. At the end of March she can compare actual results with ₦69,000 and know whether the Saturday slot worked.
Percentage of target
Progress against a target is actual ÷ target × 100. If Bisi averages ₦64,000 a week, that is 64,000 ÷ 69,000 × 100 = about 93% of target. You will use this calculation in every report.
Is the target achievable?

Achievable does not mean easy. It means that, given your baseline, your time, your money and the action you have planned, the target is reachable with real effort. A target that doubles sales in a month with no new action is a wish, and missing it again and again teaches a team to ignore targets. A target that is lower than your baseline is not a target at all. When you are unsure, start with a modest increase for one month, see what happens, then adjust. For funded projects, check that each target matches what the budget can actually pay for: you cannot train 100 women with money for 60 places.

Write the target where you will see it: at the top of your tracking sheet, in your notebook or as a pinned note on your phone. A target that is written down and looked at every week is far more likely to shape what you do.
Step 3: protect the data you collect

Tracking often means writing down information about real people: customer names and phone numbers, addresses for delivery, attendance of programme participants, sometimes ages or health details. In Nigeria, the **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023** sets rules for how personal data must be handled, and it is overseen by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC). You do not need to be a lawyer to follow good basic habits.
Collect only what you need. If you only need to count orders by area, you do not need each customer's home address in your report.
Tell people why you are collecting their details and get their agreement, especially in projects.
In reports, use totals and percentages, or codes such as 'Participant 07', instead of names.
Protect your Google account with a strong password and turn on 2-Step Verification.
When you share a sheet, give 'Viewer' access unless the person must edit, and never post the link in a public group.
Do not send screenshots of customer lists on WhatsApp groups.
Scam alert
Nobody from Google, your bank, Opay or Moniepoint needs your password or one-time code to 'verify' your account or your sheet. If someone asks for it, stop and do not share it.

Percentage change versus percentage points

This is one of the most common mistakes in reports, even professional ones. When a KPI is already a percentage, such as a conversion rate, there are two ways to describe a change, and they give very different numbers.
Conversion rose from 20% to 25%
Percentage points
Subtract: 25 minus 20
Answer: 5 percentage points
Use for rates already in %
Divide: 5 ÷ 20
Answer: 25% increase
Shows size relative to before
Both are correct, but you must say which one you mean or the reader may be misled.
A safe habit: write 'up 5 percentage points, from 20% to 25%'. Giving both the old and new numbers lets the reader see the real change for themselves.
Avoiding formula errors
**#DIV/0!** means you divided by zero, often because a month has no data yet. It disappears once data is entered.
**#VALUE!** often means a cell holds text where a number is expected, such as '2,500 naira' typed in a price column.
**#NAME?** usually means a spelling mistake in the formula name, such as =SUMIF written as =SUMIFF.
If a total looks too small, check that your range covers all rows. Using whole columns like F:F avoids this.

Rules for honest, readable charts
**Start bar and column charts at zero.** The length of a bar is how readers judge size, so cutting the axis exaggerates differences.
**Label everything.** Axis titles, units (₦, number of women, %), and the time period.
**Use the title to say the message**: 'WhatsApp brought half of March sales' is better than 'Sales by channel'.
**One message per chart.** If you want to show two points, make two charts.
**Avoid 3D effects and too many colours.** Use one strong colour for the thing you want readers to notice and grey for the rest.
**Keep the same scale** when you place two charts side by side for comparison.

Worked example: how a cut axis misleads
For example, Bisi's sales were ₦250,000 in January and ₦262,000 in February. She makes a column chart and Sheets sets the vertical axis to start at ₦240,000.
On the chart, January's bar shows only the part above ₦240,000, which is ₦10,000 tall. February's shows ₦22,000.
So February's bar looks 22,000 ÷ 10,000 = 2.2 times taller, as if sales more than doubled.
She fixes it: Chart editor, Customise, Vertical axis, and sets Min to 0.
She changes the title to 'Sales rose slightly in February (up 4.8%)'.
The corrected chart shows two bars of similar height, which matches the truth: a small, steady improvement. Her manager trusts the next chart she sends.
Line charts and the axis

For a line chart showing a trend, the vertical axis does not always have to start at zero, because readers judge the slope rather than the length. But always label the axis clearly so nobody mistakes a small wobble for a big change.
When a table beats a chart

If your reader needs exact numbers, such as a funder checking each indicator against its target, a clear table is better than a chart. A common pattern in good reports is a small table of KPIs at the top, followed by one or two charts that show the most important trend or comparison. Do not chart everything just because you can.

Pie charts deserve special care. They only work when the slices add up to a meaningful whole and there are few of them. Eight thin slices of similar size are almost impossible to compare. In that case use a bar chart sorted from largest to smallest, which shows the same information far more clearly. Avoid pie charts for changes over time completely; that is the job of a line chart.

Colours deserve a moment of thought too. If your organisation has brand colours, use them consistently: the same colour for the same thing in every chart, such as magenta always meaning WhatsApp sales. Readers then learn your charts quickly and do not have to check the legend each time.

Finally, read your chart as if you were the manager seeing it for the first time on a small phone screen. Can you read the labels? Is the main point obvious within five seconds? If not, simplify: fewer categories, larger text, a clearer title.

Trust is the most valuable thing a report carries. A manager or funder who catches one exaggerated number will doubt every number after it. Honest reporting does not mean only reporting good news. It means showing what really happened, explaining why, and saying what you will do next.

Six ways reports mislead
**Cherry-picking**: showing only the best week or the best branch and leaving out the rest.
**Changing definitions quietly**: counting enquiries as 'customers' this month when last month you only counted buyers.
**Double counting**: counting a woman twice because she attended two different trainings, then reporting 'women reached' as the total attendances.
**Hiding the denominator**: '30 women started businesses' sounds great, but out of 40 trained or out of 400?
**Claiming cause without evidence**: 'our advert increased sales by 20%' when sales also rose because of a festive season.
**Cutting the chart axis**, as you saw in the previous lesson.
Correlation is not causation

When two things rise together, it is tempting to say one caused the other. Maybe your sales rose in December because of your new flyer. Or maybe they rose because December always brings more parties, and they would have risen anyway. To make a fair claim, compare with the same period last year, or try the action in one area and not another, and see whether the results differ. When you cannot be sure, use careful words: 'sales rose after we started the flyer; part of this is likely the festive season'.

Worked example: reporting a missed target

For example, Halima's grant agreement set a target of training 100 women by the end of June. By the end of June, 82 women completed the training. Two sessions were cancelled because of heavy rain that flooded the venue.
She calculates progress: 82 ÷ 100 = 82% of target.
She does not round it up or count the women who attended only one session. Those 82 met the agreed definition of completing at least 4 of 5 sessions.
She explains the cause in one sentence: 'Two sessions in May were cancelled after the venue flooded; 23 women missed too many sessions to complete.'
She gives evidence: the attendance registers and the venue's message cancelling the bookings.
She proposes a fix: a catch-up session in July for the women who missed out, at a cost covered by unspent venue money.
Her funder sees an honest 82%, a clear reason, proof, and a practical plan. This builds far more trust than a vague 'about 100 women were reached'.
Pressure to look good

When a target is tied to money, a bonus or the next grant, people are tempted to change the counting. If you feel pressured to inflate a figure, report the true number and raise the concern with your supervisor in writing. Inflated results can lead to funds being withdrawn or repaid.
Privacy when sharing

Under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, people's personal data should be collected for a clear purpose and kept secure. In practice, for reports this means: share totals and percentages, not lists of names and phone numbers; use codes for individuals; remove columns that are not needed before sharing; and be extra careful with sensitive information such as health, religion or income. Before you share a Google Sheet, click Share and check who has access. 'Restricted' means only the people you add can open it; 'Anyone with the link' means the link works for whoever receives it, including people it is forwarded to.

Rounding is another small but real risk. Round consistently, usually to whole numbers for counts and to one decimal place for percentages, and make sure rounded parts still match the total. If three channel shares round to 51%, 35% and 15%, they add to 101%; add a short note saying figures may not add up exactly because of rounding, rather than quietly changing one of them.

Ethical reporting also means giving credit fairly. If a colleague collected the data, a partner organisation provided the venue, or a volunteer ran half of the sessions, say so. Funders and managers respect reports that are honest about who did what.

Numbers alone rarely change anything. What changes decisions is a clear explanation of what the numbers mean and what should happen next. This is the part of reporting that most people find hardest, and it is also the part that makes your work most valuable to a manager or funder.

Question
Observation (What?)

Insight (So what?)

An insight usually comes from comparing: this month against last month, one channel against another, one area against another, or results against target. Use your SUMIF breakdowns and your dashboard to look for the biggest difference, then ask why. Talk to the people involved, check customer messages, or look at what changed in that period.
Worked example: finding an insight in the data
For example, Bisi breaks her weekly sales of ₦70,000 down by day of the week using SUMIF on a Day column.
Saturday sales: ₦28,000, which is 28,000 ÷ 70,000 = 40% of the week.
Monday to Thursday together: ₦21,000, which is 30%.
Observation: Saturday alone brings in more than Monday to Thursday combined.
Insight: customers order for weekend gatherings; her 'order by Thursday for Saturday delivery' posts work well.

Recommendation: add a Friday evening delivery slot for 4 weeks, starting 3 April, and track whether Friday sales grow without reducing Saturday sales. Expected effect: raise weekly sales towards her ₦69,000 average target with no extra advertising cost.
A clear, testable recommendation backed by numbers, with a plan to measure whether it works.
Writing strong recommendations
**Specific action**: 'Call all unpaid customers' rather than 'improve debt collection'.
**Owner**: the name or role responsible.
**Deadline**: a date, not 'soon'.
**Expected effect on a KPI**: which number should move, and roughly how.
**Cost or resources**, if any, so the reader can approve it.
Reporting to a manager

A manager mostly wants to know three things: are we on track, what is going wrong, and what do you need from me. Lead with the summary and the decision you need. Keep it short, attach the dashboard, and offer more detail if asked.
Reporting to a funder

Match the length and tone to the reader. A manager in a busy shop may prefer a voice note or a short WhatsApp message with the dashboard attached. A director or board may want a two-page document. Whatever the format, keep the same order: result first, then explanation, then action. If you are unsure what your manager prefers, ask once and then stick to it.

A funder wants to see that their money achieved what was agreed. Report against the exact indicators and targets in the grant agreement or results framework, in the same order. Include outputs and outcomes, the number of people reached (with no double counting), spending against budget, evidence such as registers, photos with consent or receipts, challenges with how you handled them, and lessons learned.
Worked example: budget use in a funder report
For example, Halima's project has a total budget of ₦1,500,000 for 6 months. At the end of month 5 she has spent ₦1,200,000.
Time used: 5 ÷ 6 months = about 83%.
Spending is slightly behind time, mainly because two sessions were cancelled and the venue fee was not paid.
Remaining: ₦1,500,000 minus ₦1,200,000 = ₦300,000 for month 6, which covers the final sessions and the planned catch-up session.

Her report states: '80% of budget used at 83% of project time; underspend due to cancelled sessions; remaining ₦300,000 will fund final and catch-up sessions in June.' The funder can see that money is under control.
Ask before you move money
Many grant agreements require written approval before money is moved from one budget line to another. Check your agreement and ask your funder before spending an underspend on something new.

Funders also value honesty about lessons learned. A short section saying what you would do differently, for example 'we will confirm venues in writing two weeks ahead and keep a backup venue during the rainy season', shows that the team learns from experience. It often makes a funder more willing to support the next phase, not less.

Your capstone brings everything together. You will track a real metric for at least two to three weeks, build a dashboard, and write a report with clear interpretation, a genuine insight and a specific recommendation. The best capstones use a real business, job or community project, because real data always teaches you something a made-up example cannot.

Your capstone timeline
Week 0: confirm your goal, tracking question, three to five KPIs with definitions, baseline and one SMART target.
Weeks 1 to 3: record data daily or after each event in your Google Sheet. Run the 10-minute check each week and send yourself or your manager a weekly update.
End of week 3: complete the Summary and Dashboard tabs, with at least one honest chart.
Write the report using the seven-section structure from Lesson 4.1.
Review it with the checklist below, then share it as a PDF.
Worked example: a capstone in outline
For example, Grace runs a small hair salon in Port Harcourt. Her goal is to fill quiet weekday slots. Her tracking question: 'Are weekday bookings rising over three weeks?'
KPIs: weekday bookings per week (lagging), WhatsApp booking enquiries (leading), weekday revenue, and share of revenue from weekdays.
Baseline from her appointment book for the previous 4 weeks: 12, 10, 14 and 12 weekday bookings, an average of 48 ÷ 4 = 12 per week.
SMART target: 15 weekday bookings per week (a 25% rise, since 12 × 1.25 = 15) by the end of week 3, using a Tuesday and Wednesday discount for students.
Results: week 1, 13 bookings; week 2, 15; week 3, 17. Average 45 ÷ 3 = 15, so 100% of target.
Insight: 9 of the 17 week-3 bookings were students, and 4 of them also bought a hair product, so the discount brought extra sales as well.
Recommendation: keep the student discount for another month, and track product sales per student booking to check the offer is still profitable.
A short, honest report with real data, a clear result, a genuine insight and a specific next step: exactly what the capstone asks for.

Sharing your report

In Google Docs, choose File, then Download, then PDF document. A PDF looks the same on every phone and computer and cannot be changed by accident. Name it clearly, for example 'Grace Salon Weekday Bookings Report March 2026.pdf'. If you share a Google Docs or Sheets link instead, open Share, keep General access set to Restricted, add the reviewer's email, and choose Viewer or Commenter.
Ask for feedback
Before submitting, ask one person to read only your summary and tell you, in their own words, what happened and what you recommend. If they cannot, rewrite the summary until they can.
Next steps after the course
Keep your tracking sheet running. Three months of data is far more useful than three weeks, because you can start to see patterns.
Add one new skill at a time: pivot tables in Google Sheets (Insert, then Pivot table) for faster breakdowns, or Looker Studio for online dashboards.
Offer to prepare a monthly dashboard for your church, cooperative, association or employer. It is valuable practice and builds your reputation.
Keep your best reports, with personal data removed, as a portfolio to show future employers, clients or funders.

If your capstone results are disappointing, that is fine. The capstone is judged on the quality of your tracking and reporting, not on whether your sales went up. A clear report that says 'the target was missed, here is why, and here is what I will try next' shows exactly the skills this course teaches. What would not pass is a report with missing data, unclear definitions, or a recommendation that does not follow from the numbers.
